title: No mark, no caste
hookLine: the opening stanza says He has no mark or sign, no color, caste or lineage (Jaap 1)

lines: MARKS THAT TELL US WHERE TO PUT PEOPLE.
JAAP OPENS: NONE OF THESE APPLY.
cards: A conference badge: name, company, job title, maybe a little colored dot for vegetarian. Within two seconds of meeting someone, you've read it, and they've read yours. Plenty of life runs on marks like that.
Accent, neighborhood, last name, the logo on a shirt: little marks that tell everyone where to put you.
In the Tenth Guru's Punjab the marks were sharper still: caste, clan, the sign painted on a forehead, the cut of a robe.
And the Tenth Guru opens his great praise by taking every one of those marks and saying: none of these apply.

teach.h: NO MARK, NO SIGN, NO COLOR, NO CASTE.
teach.b: The first stanza of Jaap begins with a list of absences. Its opening words, chakr chihan ar baran jaat ar paat nahin jih, mean roughly: the One who has no mark and no sign, no color, no caste, no lineage.
Chakr is a mark, the kind of sign some religious groups wore to show which god or sect they followed. Chihan is any sign at all.
Baran is varna, the old word for the great classes of Indian society, and it also means color. Jaat is caste. Paat is lineage, the family line.
In the Guru's world, these labels decided who could eat with whom, marry whom, learn which texts, enter which temple. The stanza goes on: form, complexion, outline, dress, nobody can describe them.
So before Jaap praises a single quality, it clears the table. Whatever badge you would pin on the Divine, take it off. Here's why that lands for Sikhs.
The Gurus had been taking those same badges off people since Guru Nanak. Langar, where everyone sits in one row and eats the same food.

teach.h: CLEAR THE TABLE BEFORE THE PRAISE.
teach.b: Sangat, where anyone may sit before the Guru.
And tradition says that when he founded the Khalsa, the Tenth Guru gave its members shared names, Singh and Kaur, so a surname could no longer announce a caste.
Some Sikhs hear the opening of Jaap and the founding of the Khalsa as one idea from two sides: the One has no caste, so the people who bow to that One shouldn't wear caste either.

how: Sikhs who keep Nitnem recite this opening stanza every morning as the start of Jaap Sahib, and the Gurus' rejection of caste is lived out in langar, where all sit in one row, and in the shared Khalsa names Singh and Kaur.

o: a believer who wears no outward Sikh symbols
a hymn that cannot be written in any script
the One has no sign, caste, color or lineage

games.q: you're writing the first line of a great hymn of praise. how does Jaap Sahib begin?
o: with the One's most glorious title.
by saying what the One is not: no mark, no caste, no lineage.
games.why: Jaap opens by clearing away every label people used to sort each other, before it praises a single quality.

practice: Pick one label you use for yourself: a job title, a school, the smart one, the difficult one, the busy one.
Hold it for a breath, then set it down, like unpinning a badge and laying it on a table, and sit a while without it, asking softly who is here when that word is gone.
You don't have to answer; if you pray, you can say Waheguru once, softly.

wordCard.voice: No mark. The opening of Jaap Sahib: the One has no mark or sign, no color, caste or lineage, and no form anyone can describe.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: jaat, caste; one of the labels the first stanza of Jaap says the One does not have.
